items.answer: Tangible user interface is a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in a virtual world and that, by aligning the real world and the virtual world, provides feedback to the user's somatosensory system in place of computer-controlled haptic devices.

Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.

Object manipulation is an interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant virtual objects that uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, allows the user to change virtual arm and hand length interactively, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so distant objects can be reached quickly.

A three-dimensional widget is a simple indirect manipulation technique that places controls directly in a 3D scene with virtual objects, so manipulating a widget manipulates its associated object; each widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.

World in miniature (WIM) is an indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world. Manipulating a model object manipulates the corresponding virtual object, even if it is outside the user's reach; moving certain model objects can also change the virtual viewpoint.

questions.question: What is the goal of navigation in a virtual world?
options: A change of the user's ongoing sensory feedback or awareness
A change of the user's field of view or viewpoint
A change of the user's real-world body position or location
A change of the virtual scene's visible geometry or layout
questions.explanation: Navigation in a virtual world aims to move the user from one point to another, which appears as a change in the user's field of view or viewpoint. Changes to body position, scene geometry, or sensory feedback are not the navigation goal described.

questions.question: What two components make up the movement involved in navigation in a virtual world?
options: Travel and steering
Travel and wayfinding
Wayfinding and exploration
Locomotion and travel
questions.explanation: The movement involved in virtual navigation splits into travel and wayfinding. Locomotion names the travel part, and exploration or steering belongs to travel techniques, so those pairings do not name the two parts.

data.text: Navigation in an immersive virtual experience aims to move the user from one point to another, which changes the user's field of view or viewpoint. The movement involved is then organized into two components: travel and wayfinding.
points: Virtual-world navigation aims to move the user from one point to another, changing the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in virtual-world navigation has two parts: travel and wayfinding.

questions.question: In a virtual world, what is the travel part of navigation?
options: The selection of a route through the virtual world
The wayfinding decisions made before moving
The perception that movement has occurred
The actual movement between two locations
questions.explanation: The travel part, or locomotion, is the motor component of navigation: the user’s actual movement from one place to another. Wayfinding, route selection, and the feeling of having moved are related but not the travel part itself.

questions.question: In the travel part of navigation, what distinguishes search from exploration?
options: Search is a walking-based technique, while exploration is a steering-based technique
Search makes short precise movements, while exploration moves around to see or learn
Search has a specified target location, while exploration has no explicit target
Search relies on object manipulation, while exploration does not rely on it
questions.explanation: Search means moving to a specified target location, whereas exploration means moving without an explicit goal. Short precise movements describe maneuvering, and walking, steering, and manipulation are locomotion types rather than the travel modes being compared.

questions.question: Which broad locomotion category involves navigating by acting on things?
options: Selection-based locomotion
Walking-based locomotion
Manipulation-based locomotion
Steering-based locomotion
questions.explanation: Manipulation-based locomotion is the broad type in which navigation is done by manipulating things. The other three broad categories are not defined by acting on objects to travel.

data.text: Navigation’s travel side, called locomotion, is the actual motor movement between places, and locomotion techniques make that movement happen and perceptible in virtual worlds. That travel can serve open exploration, targeted search, or short precise maneuvering, and the techniques fall into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based families. Object manipulation is mostly absent across these families except for manipulation-based locomotion, though it is not entirely avoided in immersive implementations.
points: The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is its motor component, the actual movement between locations.
Locomotion techniques, also travel techniques, let users travel between virtual places and perceive that travel occurred.
Navigation travel can be exploration with no target, search for a target, or short precise maneuvering.
Four broad locomotion technique types are walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based.
Walking, steering, and selection may not involve object manipulation; manipulation-based uses it, though it is mostly avoided in immersive travel.

questions.question: Which locomotion technique maps physical movement in the real world to movement in a virtual world?
options: Manipulation-based locomotion
Steering-based locomotion
Walking-based locomotion
Selection-based locomotion
questions.explanation: Walking-based locomotion is defined by mapping physical walking or movement to corresponding virtual movement. The other technique types are not defined by that physical-walking mapping.

questions.question: Why do full-gait techniques limit physical walking to a bounded region?
options: Target selection is used to choose a point for virtual movement
In-place walking is mapped to a different type of virtual movement
Lateral movement is cancelled before it is mapped to virtual movement
Restricted walking is translated to any amount of virtual movement
questions.explanation: In full gait, completely free walking is not practical, so walking within a physical limit is translated into potentially unlimited virtual movement. Cancelling lateral movement and mapping in-place walking belong to other walking-based techniques.

questions.question: What is true of the user's physical movement in a partial-gait technique?
options: The user walks in a bounded region and changes physical position
The user points to a destination and changes virtual position
The user walks in place and keeps the same physical position
The user stands on a moving platform and retains physical position
questions.explanation: Partial gait has the user walk in place, so the user does not physically move forward, backward, left, or right. Bounded real-world walking is characteristic of full gait, and platform-based fixed-position setups are associated with gait negation.

questions.question: What does a gait-negation setup detect and eliminate before mapping walking to virtual navigation?
options: The user's lateral movement
The user's physical movement
The user's forward movement
The user's vertical movement
questions.explanation: Gait-negation setups remove lateral movement because natural sideways motion is hard to map to focused virtual movement. They do not remove forward movement or all physical movement.

data.text: Walking-based locomotion maps physical movement to corresponding virtual movement. It is divided into full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, which use real walking in different ways. Full gait translates limited real walking, partial gait translates walking in place, and gait negation removes lateral movement before the system maps movement to virtual navigation.
points: Walking-based locomotion maps physical movement in the real world to corresponding movement in a virtual environment.
Walking-based locomotion techniques are divided into full gait, partial gait, and gait negation categories.
Full gait techniques translate real walking into virtual movement, the most natural travel, but physical limits create a mismatch.
Partial gait techniques use specialized devices to map walking in place to virtual movement without changing physical position.
Gait negation techniques use specialized setups to cancel lateral movement, keeping physical position fixed and clarifying user intention.

questions.question: In steering-based navigation, what does the user continuously control while moving from one point to another?
options: gaze and gesture
target and route
posture and balance
direction and speed
questions.explanation: Steering-based navigation is defined by continuous control of direction and speed during movement. Gaze or gestures may be input methods in spatial steering, but they are not the continuous quantities that define the category.

questions.question: What is the main control difference between spatial steering-based and physical steering-based navigation?
options: target selection versus route planning
gaze direction versus hand gestures
walking in place versus free walking
body parts versus props or hardware
questions.explanation: Spatial steering uses the user's body parts, while physical steering uses separate hardware or vehicle-like props. The other pairs describe spatial subtypes, selection-based methods, or walking-based locomotion.

questions.question: Which spatial steering-based subtype moves the user continuously in the direction the user is looking?
options: the body-leaning directed type
the gaze-directed type
the hand-directed type
the selection-based type
questions.explanation: Gaze-directed spatial steering moves the user in the direction of looking. Hand-directed and body-leaning directed spatial steering use other body-part inputs, while selection-based locomotion uses a chosen destination rather than continuous steering.

questions.question: Which physical setup is used in physical steering-based navigation?
options: a bike locomotion platform
a pressure mat
a linear treadmill
a human-sized hamster ball
questions.explanation: Bike locomotion platforms are physical setups for steering-based travel. Pressure mats, linear treadmills, and hamster balls are setups associated with walking-based locomotion.

data.text: Steering-based navigation organizes movement by continuously controlling direction and speed while the user moves. It splits into spatial steering, where body actions direct travel, and physical steering, where vehicles or hardware direct travel. Spatial steering can use gaze, hand gestures, or body lean, while physical steering uses setups whose real steering controls direct travel in the virtual world.
points: Steering-based navigation continuously controls direction and speed while the user moves from one point to another.
Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial, controlled by body parts, and physical, controlled by vehicular props or additional hardware.
Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, hand-directed, or body-leaning directed.
Physical steering-based navigation uses physical setups or additional hardware, where physically moving the steering controls directs virtual travel.

questions.question: What kind of input is central to selection-based locomotion?
options: a continuous direction or speed of travel
a chosen endpoint or route of travel
a body lean or vehicle prop of travel
a gaze direction or hand gesture of travel
questions.explanation: Selection-based locomotion is about choosing where to go, such as an endpoint or a route, rather than continuously controlling the movement itself.

questions.question: What does route planning-based locomotion let the user specify?
options: a chosen path to the target
a continuous steering input to the target
an instant jump to the target
a miniature object drag to the target
questions.explanation: Route planning-based locomotion differs from target selection by having the user choose a route, not merely an endpoint reached instantly.

questions.question: What is manipulated in manipulation-based locomotion?
options: position, orientation, or scale in the scene
target, route, or endpoint in the scene
color, sound, or texture in the scene
direction, speed, or look in the scene
questions.explanation: Manipulation-based locomotion works by using gestures to change the user’s position, orientation, or scale, not by selecting travel endpoints or continuously steering.

questions.question: How does a world in miniature metaphor support movement?
options: object manipulation changes the viewpoint in the scene
object selection changes the route in the scene
body leaning changes the target in the scene
gaze direction changes the speed in the scene
questions.explanation: In a world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects produces a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, making the user feel as if they have moved.

data.text: Selection-based and manipulation-based locomotion are two families of travel techniques. Selection-based locomotion has the user choose a target or route; target selection moves the viewpoint to a chosen place, while route planning follows a selected path and gives more control and slightly more natural movement than target teleportation. Manipulation-based locomotion instead changes position, orientation, or scale through gestures and miniature-world object changes.
points: Selection-based locomotion lets the user choose where to go rather than steer or look continuously.
Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection and route planning.
Target selection-based locomotion can change the viewpoint to a chosen destination, using teleportation, map dragging, or the cave-system jumper.
Route planning-based locomotion lets the user select a route, giving more control and slightly more natural movement than target teleportation.
Manipulation-based locomotion can use gestures to manipulate position, orientation, or scale, combining go-go, homer, and miniature-world metaphors.

questions.question: In navigation, what distinguishes wayfinding from locomotion?
options: It specifies how quickly system content updates after input
It concerns locating oneself and choosing a path to a destination
It supplies the continuous motor movement between points
It keeps the user inside a safe real-world movement region
questions.explanation: Navigation has a motor component, locomotion or travel, and a wayfinding component. Wayfinding deals with location awareness and route selection, not with the physical act of moving or with system safety and latency.

questions.question: What role does procedural knowledge play in a wayfinding mental model?
options: It records the visual appearance of surfaces in the environment
It captures the sequence of actions needed to follow a path
It marks the safe real-world boundary where movement is allowed
It measures the latency between user input and scene update
questions.explanation: Procedural knowledge in a wayfinding mental model is the ordered sequence of actions required to follow a path. It is not about surface appearance, interaction latency, or a real-world movement boundary.

questions.question: Why does a complex virtual environment need wayfinding support even when it offers many travel techniques?
options: It lets users locate themselves and select routes to targets
It converts user gestures into continuous steering controls
It reduces the number of rendered objects and possible routes
It defines the safe real-world region where movement is allowed
questions.explanation: Travel or locomotion support alone is not enough in a complex environment; users also need location awareness and route knowledge to use available travel techniques efficiently and effectively.

questions.question: How does landmark support help a user with wayfinding?
options: It gives a map-like display that shows the whole virtual environment
It gives a trail of markers that follows earlier users' paths
It gives a directional indicator that shows space in two or three dimensions
It gives a non-mobile object that is visible from several viewpoints
questions.explanation: A good wayfinding landmark is an obvious, distinct, non-mobile object that can be seen from several different locations or viewpoints. Maps, breadcrumb trails, and direction indicators are different wayfinding supports.

data.text: Wayfinding is the mental part of navigation: it involves knowing where one is, choosing a path, and retaining usable spatial knowledge. Because this mental model is what allows users to move toward destinations, environment design should help users form it. In complex virtual environments, locomotion alone is insufficient, so designers can add supports such as landmarks, maps, paths, breadcrumbs, and direction indicators to strengthen wayfinding.
points: Navigation has locomotion and wayfinding; wayfinding is location awareness, finding destination paths, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
Wayfinding builds a mental model of the environment, so design should support it or user experience deteriorates.
Wayfinding spatial knowledge includes landmark, procedural, and topological knowledge, built through maps, real-space exploration, or model exploration.
In complex virtual environments, wayfinding support is essential; without it, travel techniques are not used efficiently or effectively.
Wayfinding supports include visible landmarks, maps, colored paths, breadcrumbs, and direction indicators.

questions.question: What is the main goal of interaction for system control in XR?
options: To select one or more virtual objects from a set
To move from one point to another in a virtual world
To issue commands that change system state or mode
To modify a virtual object's properties after selection
questions.explanation: System control is for commands that change the system's state or mode, such as launching an application or changing settings. Movement, object selection, and object manipulation are separate interaction goals.

questions.question: What makes a system-control interaction multimodal?
options: It combines multiple techniques, for example voice with gestures
It issues commands through physical buttons and switches
It presents system commands as three-dimensional widgets
It adapts a two-dimensional menu for a massive 3D environment
questions.explanation: Multimodal control works by combining input techniques, such as voice together with gestures. A 3D widget, an adapted menu, or physical buttons are single system-control methods rather than multimodal combinations.

data.text: Interaction for system control concerns the commands that change system state or mode, which cover most regular software operations. These commands can be issued through physical controllers, menus, voice, gestures, tools, or multimodal interaction techniques. Multimodal techniques combine several of these methods, for example voice with gestures.
points: Interaction for system control issues commands that change system state or mode, covering most regular software operations.
Interactive methods for system control include physical controllers, menus, voice, gestures, tools, and multimodal interaction techniques.

Maneuvering
Wayfinding

items.reason: Exploration, search, and maneuvering are types of travel in navigation, while wayfinding is the other component of navigation that supports location awareness and path finding.

Selection-Based Locomotion
Target Selection-Based Locomotion
Steering-Based Locomotion
items.reason: Walking-based, steering-based, and selection-based locomotion are broad locomotion technique types, while target selection-based locomotion is a specific type of selection-based locomotion.

items.reason: A linear treadmill, motorized floor tile, and human-sized hamster ball are specialized setups for gait negation techniques, while a pressure mat is an active walking interface associated with partial gait techniques.

questions.question: How does navigation differ from object manipulation and interaction for system control in terms of what each changes in a virtual experience?
questions.reference_answer: Navigation changes the user's location by changing the virtual viewpoint, and it mostly does not involve object manipulation. Object manipulation changes the properties of a selected virtual object, such as its position, orientation, or scale. Interaction for system control issues commands that change the system's state or mode, such as settings or applications.

questions.question: Why is wayfinding support essential in a complex virtual environment even when a system provides many locomotion techniques?
questions.reference_answer: Wayfinding aims to build a mental model of the surroundings and of the path to a destination, so that the user can locate themselves and choose a suitable path. Environment design should support this mental map. Without wayfinding support, travel techniques cannot be used efficiently or effectively, and the overall user experience deteriorates.

questions.question: How does route planning-based locomotion create movement differently from target selection-based locomotion?
questions.reference_answer: In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination and the viewpoint changes to make the user feel moved there, as in teleportation or map dragging. In route planning-based locomotion, the user selects a route to the target, and different viewpoint changes along that route make the user feel movement along a path. This gives more granular control and slightly more natural movement than teleportation.

questions.question: How do spatial steering-based navigation and physical steering-based navigation differ in how the user controls direction and speed?
questions.reference_answer: Both types continuously control direction and speed while the user moves. Spatial steering uses body-based signals, such as gaze, hand gestures, or body lean, to determine travel. Physical steering uses separate hardware or setups, such as bike locomotion platforms or VR simulators, where moving the controls changes virtual travel.
